summary: Defines a set of extended status codes for the mail system, used in delivery status reports, tracking and diagnostics. Together with Delivery Status Notifications, they allow delivery results to be shown in a way that does not depend on language or media.

eli5.summary: Mail errors like it failed are not very helpful. This note defines a detailed code system, like 5.1.1, that says exactly what went wrong in any language.

questions: what are smtp enhanced status codes
what does the second digit of an email status code mean
subtitle: A three-part number like 5.1.1 that says, in any language, why a mail message was or was not delivered.

tldr.problem: SMTP reply codes are too few and too overloaded to describe mail delivery results in a machine-readable, language-independent way.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3463 defines status codes of the form class.subject.detail, such as 2.1.23. The class says success or failure, the subject says where the problem likely lies, and the detail gives the precise condition.
tldr.outcome: It is a Draft Standard that replaced RFC 1893 and has since been updated by RFC 3886, RFC 4468, RFC 4865, RFC 4954 and RFC 5248.

today: RFC 3463 is a Draft Standard that obsoleted RFC 1893. It has been updated by RFC 3886, RFC 4468, RFC 4865, RFC 4954 and RFC 5248.

sections.title: Why SMTP Codes Were Not Enough
sections.content:
Mail systems need a standard way to report errors that is richer than SMTP reply codes and the system-specific text in mail messages. Enhanced mail system status codes are meant for delivery status notifications (DSNs, defined in RFC 3464) and give a machine-readable status that does not depend on any human language.

The RFC says SMTP provides only about 12 useful codes for delivery reports. Most SMTP codes are protocol responses such as the 354 reply to the DATA command, and each of the 12 useful ones is overloaded to mean several different error conditions. The remaining SMTP number space is too small, and consuming it would also reduce the codes available for new ESMTP extensions.

The new codes build on the SMTP theory of reply codes. They keep its success, permanent error and transient error meaning in the first value and use the second value for a finer classification, which also separates mailbox errors from host errors.
sections.eli5: The old mail error numbers were like having only twelve words to describe every possible problem. This note adds a much bigger vocabulary so mail systems can say exactly what happened.

sections.title: Structure of a Status Code
sections.content:
A status code has three numeric fields separated by dots: class.subject.detail. The class is 2, 4 or 5. The subject and detail are each one to three digits, written without leading zeros. White space and comments are not allowed inside a code. The RFC's example is 2.1.23.

The first number says whether the delivery attempt worked, the second says the probable source of any trouble, and the third names the precise condition. These codes are for media and language independent reporting, not for system-specific diagnostics.

2.X.X Success
The DSN reports a positive delivery action. Detail codes may note transformations needed for delivery.
4.X.X Persistent transient failure
The message is valid, but a temporary condition caused delivery to be delayed or abandoned. Sending again later may succeed.
5.X.X Permanent failure
Resending the message as it is is not likely to help. The message or the destination must change.
sections.eli5: The code is like an address with three parts: first whether it worked, then what part of the mail system is involved, then the exact problem. You can read it even if you do not speak the sender's language.

sections.title: The Eight Subject Categories
sections.content:
The second number, the subject, sorts problems by where they probably come from and who can fix them. Each subject applies to all three classes.

  • X.0.XXX other or undefined status, with no more subject information.
  • X.1.XXX addressing: the originator or destination address, including syntax and validity. The sender can generally correct these and retry.
  • X.2.XXX mailbox: assumed to be under the recipient's control.
  • X.3.XXX mail system: the destination system, assumed to be under its administrator's control.
  • X.4.XXX network and routing: infrastructure such as directory and routing services.
  • X.5.XXX mail delivery protocol: implementation errors or an unreliable connection.
  • X.6.XXX message content or media: translation, transcoding or unsupported media. Sender and receiver must support a common set of content types.
  • X.7.XXX security or policy: filtering and cryptographic operations, under the control of the sender, the recipient or both.
sections.eli5: The middle number says whose turn it is to fix things: the person who wrote the address, the owner of the mailbox, the mail computer, the network, and so on.

sections.title: Registering and Interpreting Codes
sections.content:
The code space can be extended only by standards track documents. Servers should send only defined, registered status codes, and a system with its own error types should map them as closely as possible to the standard ones. System-specific diagnostics should travel by other means, not in status codes.

Published codes are not meant to be redefined or removed. Clients keep the space extensible by following two rules. A client must recognize and report the class even when it does not know the subject. If it knows the subject but not the detail, it must still report the subject, giving the general error that the subject describes.
sections.eli5: If your mail program meets a number it has never seen, it falls back to the part it does understand, like knowing a word starts with the right letters even if you cannot read the rest.

sections.title: The Enumerated Detail Codes
sections.content:
The RFC lists detail codes under each subject. A few examples show the style:

  • X.1.1 bad destination mailbox address: the part left of the @ does not exist. Useful only for permanent failures.
  • X.1.2 bad destination system address: the part right of the @ is invalid for mail.
  • X.2.2 mailbox full: the user has exceeded a quota. Should be used as a persistent transient failure.
  • X.3.4 message too big for system. Useful only as a permanent error.
  • X.4.4 unable to route: no next hop could be determined. One example is a DNS lookup that returns only an SOA record for a domain name.
  • X.4.7 delivery time expired. If possible, the code for the actual problem found at delivery time should be returned instead.
  • X.7.1 delivery not authorized, message refused. Useful only as a permanent error.

Each subject also has a catch-all X.n.0 for cases that fit no other detail code. Appendix A of the RFC collects all the codes in one list.
sections.eli5: Under each category there is a list of specific problems, like mailbox full, address does not exist, or message too big. Each has its own last number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security section is short. More precise status codes may disclose more information about how an internal mail system is implemented than was available before.

The RFC does add security and policy codes, for example X.7.5 cryptographic failure and X.7.7 message integrity failure, but these only report problems; the document does not define a security mechanism.
sections.eli5: The more exactly a mail system explains what went wrong, the more it also tells strangers about how it is built. That is the one risk the RFC points out.

data.title: Status code grammar
data.code:
status-code = class "." subject "." detail
class = "2"/"4"/"5"
subject = 1*3digit
detail = 1*3digit
